results.title: Deep Structural Causal Models for Counterfactual Mesh Generation - Rajat Rasal
results.content:
ent of Computing Imperial College London
695 subscribers

633 views
3 Aug 2021
Causality allows us to follow a natural line of reasoning by asking questions. It allows us to see, "What does Twitter tell me about the state of the World?", it allows us to intervene, "What if I stopped taking my medication, will I feel better?", and above all, it allows us to imagine, "If I hadn’t worked as hard, would I have done as well?". It is, however, on these more challenging queries that conventional statistical tools fall short. Although they excel in the purely associative domain, unless imbued with additional techniques from causality, they cannot tackle problems at the interventional or counterfactual level. 

In this project, we build causal models, using deep learning techniques, which are capable of answering questions at all levels of the causal hierarchy. Our implementation uses the Deep Structural Causal Model (DSCM) framework to achieve tractable inference of counterfactuals. Through our experiments, we bridge the gap between traditional statistics and deep structural causal modelling. Our key contribution is the application of the DSCM framework to model the causal generative process of subcortical meshes in the UK Biobank, allowing us to produce medically reasonable, realistic, counterfactual brain stem and hippocampus meshes.

Project report: https://bit.ly/3rkBjR3

results.title: causality - Causal Bayesian network, causal diagram, structural causal model and marginal structural model: what do they exactly mean? - Cross Validated
results.content: **Question 1**: What is the difference between *causal diagrams* and *causal Bayesian network*? In a probabilistic Bayesian network, the arrows into Y mean that the probability of Y is governed by the conditional probability tables for Y, given observations of its parent variables. The same is true for causal Bayesian networks, except that the conditional probability tables specify the probability of Y given interventions on the parent variables. The arrows simply mean Y is a function of its parents, as well as the exogenous variable $U\_Y$: $$ Y = f\_Y(X, A, B, C,…, U\_Y)$$ (...) To turn a noncausal Bayesian network into a causal model—or, more precisely, to make it capable of answering counterfactual queries—we need a dose-response relationship at each node. While I understand the need of a model that use a dose-response relationship in order to do counterfactuals, I do not see the difference between the *SCMs*, defined above by Pearl, and the *causal structural model*, defined in this book, by Hernan and Robins. Addition of do-calculus provides one of the ingredient of a causal model, i.e., as Pearl states, making them to answer counterfactual queries. I will give my answer based on Pearl's other book (Causality). * For interventional queries, you also need a directed graph (e.g. a Bayesian Network(BN), and especially a Causal Bayesian Network(CBN).) As you quoted, CBNs are required to be able to see how the variables influence each other (hence a graph is used). This provides all we need to answer your first question **Answer to question 1:** **TL;DR: SCM = causal diagram + functions for each edge** The causal diagram is a graph that describes what variables relate to each other, whereas an SCM **additionally gives a quantitative description of these relationships,**. Given the joint distribution, we can answer **conditional probability questions**. However, we are not able to answer any **causal or interventional questions**. For example, we cannot answer, if $Y$ is forced to be 2, what would the distribution of $X$ be. This is an example where two SCMs can have the same interventional graph and joint distribution but different counterfactual outcomes. Argument on Interactions in The Book of Why. Achieving Counterfactual Fairness with Imperfect Structural Causal Model. #### Abstract. Counterfactual fairness alleviates the discrimination between the model prediction toward an individual in the actual world (observational data) and that in counterfactual world (i.e., what if the individual belongs to other sensitive groups). The existing studies need to pre-define the structural causal model that captures the correlations among variables for counterfactual inference; however, the underlying causal model is usually unknown and difficult to be validated in real-world scenarios. Moreover, the misspecification of the causal model potentially leads to poor performance in model prediction and thus makes unfair decisions. In this research, we propose a novel minimax game-theoretic model for counterfactual fairness that can produce accurate results meanwhile achieve a counterfactually fair decision with the relaxation of strong assumptions of structural causal models. In addition, we also theoretically prove the error bound of the proposed minimax model.
